content: Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is frequently diagnosed at an advanced stage, necessitating primary cytoreductive surgery followed by combination chemotherapy as the standard first-line treatment. The current standard chemotherapy regimen for EOC involves a platinum-based combination, typically carboplatin and paclitaxel (PAC/carbo). Pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD) is a modified formulation of doxorubicin that has been developed to reduce the severity and frequency of side effects compared to conventional doxorubicin. Recent evidence suggests that PLD, when combined with carboplatin, can improve progression-free survival in women with relapsed, platinum-sensitive EOC. This raises the question of whether PLD offers any survival advantage when used as part of first-line treatment. The objective of this study was to assess the role of PLD, either alone or in combination with other agents, in the first-line chemotherapy of women with EOC. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group's Trial Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies from January 1990 to February 2013. Additional searches included online trial registries and abstracts from relevant scientific meetings starting from 2000. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing PLD-based regimens to other chemotherapy regimens in women with EOC, regardless of whether they had undergone primary cytoreductive surgery, were included. Two large RCTs were identified and included in the analysis. The first trial compared a three-weekly regimen of PLD and carboplatin (PLD/carbo) with the standard PAC/carbo regimen in 820 women with EOC (stages Ic to IV). The second trial involved 1726 women with stage III/IV EOC and compared four experimental arms, one of which included PLD in combination with PAC/carbo, to the standard PAC/carbo regimen. In this trial, PLD was administered every six weeks (alternating cycles). The two trials were not combined in a meta-analysis due to differences in their designs, but both were deemed to have a low risk of bias. In the first trial, no statistically significant differences were observed between the PLD/carbo and PAC/carbo groups in terms of progression-free survival (PFS) (hazard ratio [HR] 1.01, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.85 to 1.19) or overall survival (OS) (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.13). However, severe anaemia (risk ratio [RR] 2.74, 95% CI 1.54 to 4.88) and thrombocytopenia (RR 8.09, 95% CI 3.93 to 16.67) were significantly more common in the PLD/carbo group. Conversely, alopecia (RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.14) and severe neurotoxicity (RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.66) were significantly more frequent in the PAC/carbo group. Quality of life scores did not differ significantly between the two groups. In the second trial, which compared the alternating triplet regimen (PLD/PAC/carbo) to PAC/carbo, no significant differences in PFS (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.09) or OS (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.08) were reported. However, the triplet regimen was associated with a significantly higher incidence of severe hematological toxicities, including anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and febrile neutropenia, compared to the standard PAC/carbo regimen. No RCTs were identified that evaluated single-agent PLD as a first-line treatment for EOC. In conclusion, the combination of PLD and carboplatin (PLD/carbo) represents a viable alternative to the standard PAC/carbo regimen for first-line treatment of EOC. While PLD/carbo may result in more frequent dose delays and treatment discontinuations, it could be a preferable option for women seeking to avoid alopecia or those at high risk of neurotoxicity. However, the alternating triplet regimen (PLD/PAC/carbo) does not appear to confer any survival benefit and is associated with increased toxicity, limiting its potential for further investigation. Additional research is needed to determine the optimal PLD/carbo regimen that balances safety and efficacy for newly diagnosed EOC.
